attempts.entry_title: Electrically evoked EEG and cortico-thalamic spiking in head-fixed mice (Claar, Rembado et al. 2023)
attempts.summary: Most depth and state effects held in this data: superficial stimulation gave smaller ERPs and lower PCIst than deep, and PCIst was higher awake than under isoflurane at 30 of 30 sites. The late ERP peak was not absent with superficial stimulation (0 to 2 of 12 sites lacked it), and spiking outside the stimulated area was not limited to deep stimulation. Thalamus led cortex in the rebound by far less than reported, and burst correlations with cortical rate were weaker. Laminar CSD and stimulation depth could not be tested because the files hold no layers or electrode depth. Figure 4 unit counts are one third of the legend's, probably because it counts each unit once per current.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Claar, Rembado et al. (2023) on dandiset 000458, which holds skull EEG from 23 mice, with Neuropixels LFP and sorted units from 17 of them, during single-pulse electrical stimulation of superficial or deep layers of MOs or SSp, awake, under isoflurane and in recovery. One notebook tests the ERP duration and magnitude, the peaks of the ERP and PCIst across depths and states; a second tests the spiking responses of stimulated and other cortex and of somatomotor thalamus, bursts, latencies and their trial-by-trial relation to the late ERP; a third computes the LFP and CSD magnitudes of the example session of Figure 3 and times those of Figure 3D. The CSD claims by cortical layer (Figure 6A) are not tested.

outcomes.statement: Deep (layer 5/6) stimulation in the awake state usually evokes an ERP with two prominent peaks, near 25 ms and near 180 ms; the late component is not evident with superficial stimulation, in MOs or SSp.

The late GFP peaks of superficial sites are smaller than those of deep sites (per-site table) but above z = 3.

outcomes.statement: Stimulating superficial MOs evoked a local spike, LFP and CSD response followed by quiescence of 94.2 +/- 16.1 ms in MO neurons, with minimal to no responses in other sampled areas.
outcomes.source: Results, The spiking response pattern of the stimulated cortex echoes the ERP, paragraph 2; Figure 2C and 2D to 2F, left
outcomes.quote: Stimulating superficial MOs evoked a local spike, LFP and CSD response, followed by a period of quiescence lasting 94.2±16.1 ms in MO neurons
outcomes.notes: Two superficial MOs sites have units (571619, 575102). Reading (a), MO RS population rate below its -2 to 0 s mean after 25 ms, high current, all awake trials, 1 ms bins; 84.0 +/- 25.0 ms (59 and 109 ms). outcomes.statement: The triphasic pattern of deep stimulation is replicated, shifted in time, in SM-TH; a brief excitation (peak 22.3 +/- 3.2 Hz), 74.6 +/- 15.5 ms of suppression, and rebound excitation (peak 14.7 +/- 1.0 Hz). It is absent with superficial stimulation.

outcomes.quote: we observed a brief excitation (peak population firing rate 22.3±3.2 Hz), a 74.6±15.5 ms long period of suppression, followed by rebound excitation (peak population firing rate 14.7±1.0 Hz). This is not the case when stimulating superficial layers
outcomes.notes: 14 deep sites have SM-TH units; 12 of 14 are triphasic (high current, all awake, 1 ms). The suppression is 59.5 to 100.7 ms, within 74.6 +/- 15.5 in most readings, but the early (13 to 32 Hz) and rebound (14.7 to 21.7 Hz) peaks are never within tolerance together. With superficial stimulation, 3 or 4 of 4 sites have no SM-TH unit significantly increased at 150 to 300 ms (reading b); by reading (a) 1 to 3 of 4 have no rebound peak above z = 3. Requiring at least 10 ms below baseline gives the same counts of triphasic sites in every reading.

outcomes.statement: In the example deep MOs session, evoked LFP, CSD and spiking magnitudes are large near the stimulation site (54.0, 51.4 and 30.9 SD.s in MO) and smaller in distant VIS (18.0, 4.8 and 1.8 SD.s).
outcomes.source: Results, Global ERPs are associated with widespread evoked cortical activity, paragraph 1; Figure 3A to 3C
outcomes.quote: The magnitude of the LFP near the stimulation site is greater than background activity (54.0 SD∙s in MO) and decays with distance from the stimulation site (18.0 SD∙s in VIS
outcomes.notes: The magnitudes average all channels of a region "except layer 1"; the channel locations are CCF areas without layers (MOs, SSp-ll, ...). The LFP, CSD and shuffle pipeline was run for the example session (571619, deep MOs; MO on probe F, 119 valid channels; VIS on probe C, 87), with layer 1 approximated by the top 100 um of each area and also without the exclusion (claar_lfp.ipynb). Over 128 combinations of readings MO exceeds VIS for all three signals in 112; the LFP order reverses in 4 of 32 LFP readings (high current, 1 Hz, -0.5 to 0 s baseline). No combination puts all six values within tolerance, and at most three are (medium current, 0.1 Hz, top 100 um left out, -2 to 0 s, epoch shuffle, 5 ms kernel, spiking as |z|; LFP 60.83 and 21.75, CSD 48.77 and 5.21, spiking 28.75 and 2.76, against 54.0, 18.0, 51.4, 4.8, 30.9 and 1.8). The LFP magnitude in MO is never within tolerance (7.57 to 77.16). Leaving out the top 100 um changes no ordering and moves the CSD values by up to 2.84. The spiking magnitude as the Methods describe it (signed z) is 0.31 to 3.96 in MO; integrating |z| gives 28.31 to 31.37 with the 5 ms kernel and the -2 to 0 s baseline, so the signed integral, in which the suppression cancels the excitation, most likely explains the earlier values far below 30.9 (verifier, round 2). Only the ordering is reproduced; the measured values are those of the combination named above, one of two with three values within tolerance.
deviations: Layer 1 is not labelled in the files; it is approximated by the channels in the top 100 um of each area (an assumed thickness), and the result is shown with and without the exclusion.

The Chebyshev channel rejection is applied once per channel (no channel was rejected), where the Methods apply it per sample and epoch; the CSD is computed from the trial-averaged LFP on rows of two channels, smoothed over 13 then 2 rows for the Methods' 26 then 4 channels; decimation and high pass are zero phase; the recording-wide shuffle draws onsets over the span of the awake pulses.

The spiking magnitude is shown both as the signed integral of the Methods and as the integral of |z| (Results, Global ERPs..., paragraph 1, "our magnitude metric accounts for both reductions as well as increases").

outcomes.notes: The size of the LFP and CSD computation was measured (claar_lfp.ipynb). Figure 3D needs 86 probe areas over 24 stimulation sites; at the rate measured on the example's two probes, which varies from run to run, this takes 234 to 265 min with all readings, and reading the LFP alone 86 to 92 min (71 to 76 min if the areas of one probe share a read), over the runs made for this record, over the 30 min notebook limit. The estimate is rough (it scales the shuffles by samples, and counts the ACSF channels once per area), but even the read-once figure is more than twice the limit. Split across notebooks of under 30 min it would need about eight; that is left to a later attempt. Layer 1 can be approximated as in fig3abc-decay-with-distance, so the missing layers do not block the claim; its size does. The spiking part was computed for every site (claar_spikes.ipynb). With the signed z of the Methods no group median is near the paper's and no stimulated group is significantly above zero after correction. With |z| the paper's significance pattern for spiking holds in 27 of 32 shuffled rows, and with the 5 ms kernel and the -2 to 0 s baseline at the medium current the deep stimulated median is 27.96 to 29.18 (29.3 +/- 2.93) and the deep non-stimulated median 4.18 to 6.25 (4.4 +/- 0.44), but the superficial stimulated median is 4.81 to 4.86 against 1.8.

outcomes.statement: Figure 4 rests on 870 RS units from stimulated and 4110 from non-stimulated cortex in 7 mice with superficial stimulation, and 2559 and 9363 in 17 mice with deep stimulation.
outcomes.source: Figure 4 legend
outcomes.quote: Panels A–C are derived from 870 RS neurons from stimulated cortex and 4110 RS neurons from non-stimulated cortical regions in N=7 mice and panels D–F from 2559 RS neurons from stimulated cortex and 9363 RS neurons from non-stimulated cortical regions in N=17 mice
outcomes.notes: The files hold 290 and 1370 RS units in stimulated and other ipsilateral cortex over the 7 superficial sites, and 853 and 3162 over the 17 deep sites (16 mice). These are exactly one third of the legend's 870, 4110 and 2559, and 1.3% above a third of its 9363. The site counts (7 and 17) match the legend's N. With presence ratio > 0.9 the counts are 221, 1020, 665 and 2421. The factor of three suggests the legend counts each unit once per current or per time window; the paper does not say. Counting each unit once per current with valid awake trials (all 24 sites with units have three currents) gives 870, 4110, 2559 and 9486 RS units, the legend's first three counts exactly and within tolerance of the fourth, and 204, 609, 447 and 1554 FS units against 180, 585, 387 and 1422. This reading is not in the claims file; it is asked of a reader (questions/000458.yaml) and the outcome stays on the claims file's count.

outcomes.statement: In the initial excitation window (2 to 25 ms), the fraction of activated RS neurons is always higher in stimulated cortex than elsewhere; across 24 animals an average of 0.5% (0 to 2.6%) of neurons in non-stimulated regions were modulated against 17.8% (0 to 83.3%) in stimulated cortex, and about three times more cortical neurons respond to deep than to superficial stimulation.
outcomes.source: Results, Global ERPs are associated with widespread evoked cortical activity, paragraph 4; Figure 4A and 4D; Results, The spiking response pattern of the stimulated cortex echoes the ERP, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Indeed, across all 24 animals, only an average of 0.5% (minimum 0% and maximum 2.6%) of the neurons was modulated in the initial excitation, compared to an average of 17.8% (minimum 0% and maximum 83.3%) in stimulated cortex
outcomes.notes: Over 16 combinations of readings (current, awake trials, pre-stimulus window, FDR family), the mean fraction of modulated RS units at 2 to 25 ms is 2.4 to 5.1% per non-stimulated region (maximum 29 to 50%) and 24 to 39% in stimulated cortex (maximum 83 to 100%), against 0.5% (2.6%) and 17.8% (83.3%). The fraction increased in stimulated cortex does not exceed the other areas at every site in any reading. The deep over superficial ratio of modulated fractions is between 2 and 4 in 15 of 16 readings. Measured is the first reading (high current, all awake, adjacent window, per-site FDR). With the three currents pooled (unit x current, a variant outside the claims file), 2.6 to 3.2% of non-stimulated and 26 to 29% of stimulated RS units are modulated.
deviations: The pre-stimulus window and the FDR family are not given; both readings of each were run.

attempts.entry_title: Shunting inhibition, synchrony and entropy in Neuropixels recordings and a network model (Burman et al. 2023)
attempts.summary: The paper's central patch-clamp findings, that synaptic GABAA receptor reversal is more depolarized and inhibition shunting in awake cortex and that blocking local network activity undoes this, could not be tested, as those recordings are not deposited. Its Neuropixels finding that neurons are less synchronous and more variable in spike timing awake than under isoflurane held up in direction and test, with means slightly off. Exact numbers come out only with the firing rate the paper's code computes, not the Methods' rate (144 units excluded against 203). The network model's shunting inhibition gave lower synchrony, higher entropy and better decoding in every run, two means just outside tight tolerances. Higher awake firing and the rate-regressed control also held.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Burman, Brodersen, Raimondo, Sen and Akerman (2023) that can be tested on dandiset 000458, the Allen Institute Neuropixels recordings with cortical electrical stimulation awake and under isoflurane that the paper reuses (Figure 4A to 4D, Figure S6), and runs the paper's network model (Figure 4E to 4H, Figure S7). The paper's gramicidin patch-clamp recordings (Figures 1 to 3) are not in the dandiset nor deposited elsewhere.

outcomes.statement: Responses of networks with shunting E_GABAAR to 100 different input patterns are decoded more accurately by a downstream classifier.
outcomes.source: Results, Shunting inhibition promotes local network desynchronization and response flexibility, paragraph 2; Figure S7 (not read); Methods, Characterization of stimulus-evoked spiking responses, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: when we assessed a network’s ability to encode different patterned inputs, we observed that networks with shunting E GABAAR could be more accurately decoded by a downstream classifier
outcomes.notes: Mean decoding accuracy 0.9848 shunting against 0.9315 hyperpolarizing (chance 0.01). D1, paired t test of the 20 per-run accuracies, t = 16.42, p = 1.11e-12 in this execution; D2, shunting higher in 20 of 20 runs. The spike counts the classifier uses are small integers, and in 0.80 to 0.81 of the test trials under shunting and 0.90 to 0.92 under hyperpolarizing the fifth-nearest training trial is at the same distance as the sixth, so the accuracy depends on how ties are broken, which differs between runners. Executions on different runners, with the same per-run rate, entropy and synchrony, printed t = 16.92, p = 6.52e-13 (the first execution and the one verifier round 2 read) and t = 16.42, p = 1.11e-12 (the round-1 revision and this one). With tied neighbours chosen by five other random orders of the training trials, a run's accuracy moves by at most 0.0020 (shunting) and 0.0045 (hyperpolarizing), D1 gives t = 16.35 to 17.22 (p at most 1.20e-12) and D2 holds in 20 of 20 runs each time, so the outcome does not depend on the tie-breaking.
deviations: Seeds are fixed (1 to 20, one per run) where the gist sets none, so the runs are other draws of the paper's model; this cannot change the model, only the sample.

The stimulus is held as one periodic 2,500 ms set instead of the gist's 4 GB whole-run array, to fit in memory; a small run with both gives identical spike trains, and the gist itself run unmodified on that small run gives the same spikes and the same per-neuron rate, entropy and synchrony (data check).

The cross-validation shuffle is seeded with the run's seed (the gist sets none). The seeds fix the spikes and the folds but not the accuracy exactly, as the classifier's ties between equally distant trials are broken differently on different runners; the notebook shows D1 and D2 under five other tie-breaking orders, and all give the same outcome.

outcomes.statement: In a multi-compartment model, the differences in membrane properties between states do not explain the differences in measured synaptic E_GABAAR.
outcomes.source: Results, Awake cortex exhibits more depolarized synaptic EGABAAR and shunting fast synaptic inhibition, paragraph 3; Results, Network activity in awake cortex raises synaptic EGABAAR, paragraph 2; Figure S4 (not read); Methods, Simulating measurements of synaptic EGABAAR
outcomes.quote: modeling of synaptic GABA A R responses in biologically realistic neurons confirmed that differences in synaptic E GABAAR could not be explained by the intrinsic membrane properties in anesthetized and awake cortices
outcomes.notes: The claim rests on the paper's NEURON model of an L2/3 pyramidal neuron and a Matlab analysis of its simulated ramps (github.com/richardjburman/burman-et-al-2022---Awake-EGABAAR at commit a404c3e, hoc files and NEURON_Egaba_Analysis.m). The model is public and the Methods ("Simulating measurements of synaptic EGABAAR", Table 2) give its membrane properties per state, the synapses, the E_GABA values (-85 to -35 mV in 5 mV steps) and the ramp protocol, so the ramp estimates could be simulated under the anesthetized and awake properties. What is open is what they would be compared with. The measure Figure S4 shows and the comparison behind "could not be explained" are in the Figure S4 legend, which was not in the text read, and the claims file gives no criterion; a choice such as the estimation error under each state's properties against the measured difference of Figure 2H would be arbitrary. So the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified and was not simulated (a further obstacle, the analysis is Matlab, and NEURON is not in the entry's environment). The question is for the paper's authors (findings, methods_unavailable). Neither part uses the dandiset.

paper_notes.statement: The paper's analysis code computes the evoked firing rate used for the exclusion (below 0.1 Hz or above 200 Hz) as the sum of the spikes' latencies in ms (np.sum of spike_times) over trials times 10 ms, where the Methods describe an average evoked firing rate. With this rate the dataset gives the paper's sample exactly (662 kept, 203 excluded, median 34 per recording, 1 to 93) and its Figure 4D means (synchrony 0.325 and 0.393, entropy 1.347 and 1.111); with the spike-count rate it gives 721 kept and 144 excluded. The 200 Hz bound thus acted on spike-count rates near 45 Hz.

Version 0.230317.0039 holds 18 files with units and electrical stimulation awake and under isoflurane; the paper uses 17. sub-599017_ses-20220210 (943 units, SSp stimulation, 718 awake and 720 isoflurane valid trials) is not in the paper's code list, and the paper does not say why. The Methods select regular spiking units with a waveform duration of 0.4 ms or more, the code more than 0.4 ms, and the Methods name the areas SSp-ll, SSp-tr and MOs where the code takes every unit whose location begins with the stimulated region. Neither difference changes the units selected in this dataset.

attempts.entry_title: Thalamic feedback and cortical stimulation responses (Russo, Claar, Furregoni et al. 2025)
attempts.summary: The paper's central finding held in this data: late EEG, LFP and CSD responses to motor cortex stimulation in mice are larger at rest than during running, as are the human responses in the paper's Source Data. During running, thalamic baseline firing roughly doubled as reported, but evoked thalamic firing rose only when trials were pooled across sessions. The thalamic rebound did not lead the cortical one, and relay units showed no split into high- and low-firing groups, so most claims built on that split failed. Optogenetic thalamic inhibition delayed the rebound but failed one of six tests, and the model could not be run within the time limit. The dataset holds 10 of the paper's 26 mouse sessions.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Russo, Claar, Furregoni et al. (2025) on dandiset 000458, which holds EEG, Neuropixels LFP and units, wheel speed and trial tables from 24 sessions of cortical electrical stimulation in mice; ten sessions have the deep MOs stimulation the paper analyses. It compares the late evoked response at rest and during running in EEG, LFP and CSD, the thalamic and cortical spiking that accompanies it, and the human claims on the paper's Source Data file. A second notebook tests the optogenetic claims on the paper's figshare deposit.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds part of the paper's mouse data: 10 sessions from 10 mice with deep MOs stimulation (9 with Neuropixels), where the paper reports EEG from 26 sessions of 15 mice and units from 21 mice. The posterior stimulation sessions of Figure S6 (12 sessions, 6 mice) are not in it, and the optogenetic sessions are on figshare. The dataset's description cites Claar et al. 2023 and does not say which sessions Russo et al. 2025 used.
The units' waveform_duration is described as the mean duration in seconds; its values (0.11 to 2.07) are milliseconds.

The trial table's is_running marks a trial as running when the mean speed from -0.5 to +0.5 s is above 0 cm/s, as its description says; the paper uses 0.1 cm/s. The classification here was recomputed from running_speed, and agrees with is_running at 0 cm/s for every trial.

The EEG, the LFP, the units and the trial table share a clock: each trial onset is within 0.4 ms of an EEG and LFP sample, in the raw trial-averaged signals the stimulation artifact sits within 0.2 ms of the onset in the EEG and within 0.6 ms (1.5 samples at 2.5 kHz) in the LFP of every session, and units fire at 18 to 41 Hz in 2 to 10 ms after the pulse against 2 to 7 Hz before it, in every mouse.

Besides the deep MOs sessions, the dandiset holds superficial MOs and SSp stimulation sessions that the paper's analysis does not use; nothing in the files marks the sessions or the trials and channels the paper kept. The is_valid and is_data_valid flags are the files' own.

In the optogenetic deposit the four protocol folders of each probe list the same cluster_ids, with the same peak channel, duration, area and quality metrics for every unit (1432 of 1432), so they are cut from one spike sort and units can be paired across protocols by cluster_id.

paper_notes.statement: The depth of the stimulating electrode is 1.06 +- 0.05 mm below the surface in the Results and 1.4 +- 0.24 mm below the brain surface in the Methods.

Question for the authors: how was the 127.8 +- 4.1 ms silence of the triphasic pattern measured? Neither the first rebound spike latency minus 10 ms (171.5 ms for RS, 160.8 ms for relay units here) nor the time below baseline minus 2 SD (57.9 and 71.4 ms) gives it.

Question for the authors: what is the unit of the rest against active tests of evoked firing rate (Figures 3A, S9A, S10A)? The legends say across subjects, the Source Data hold unequal numbers of rest and active values (per trial), and the code compares per-session medians. Here the SM-TH increase is significant per trial (p = 0.00054) and not per unit (p = 0.41) or per mouse (p = 0.30), and the FS decrease is significant per unit and per mouse but not per trial. Within sessions (van Elteren) the SM-TH increase gives p = 0.19 and the FS decrease p = 1.3e-08.

Question for the authors: which baseline window sets the GFP peak threshold of the EEG, LFP and CSD latencies (Figure 2B), and how are the two columns of a Neuropixels probe handled in the CSD depth smoothing of 26 and 4 channels? Here the baseline was -1 to -0.01 s and the two sites of a row were averaged; both are assumptions.

The optogenetic deposit (figshare 28440311 v1) has no description of its layout or of the event the spike latencies are timed from; one mouse's unit tables (673553) lack the area column, and it holds no LFP, so the LFP latencies of Figure 2G cannot be checked. It has light-over-MOs sessions in five mice, where the Figure S8B legend reports two.
